query: How can we measure and model retailer behavior, price markups, and potential voucher-driven inflation; what market-level data and IV/event-study approaches separate supply vs demand?

response.query: How can we measure and model retailer behavior, price markups, and potential voucher-driven inflation; what market-level data and IV/event-study approaches separate supply vs demand?
response.answer: To measure retailer behavior and price markups, use market-level data and instrumental variable approaches. Event studies can separate supply from demand effects. Voucher-driven inflation can be modeled using price elasticity and consumer response data.

results.title: Transparency in Coverage - Federal Register
results.content: For instance, as noted in the preamble to the proposed rule, research shows patients saved $7.9 million and issuers saved $36 million on imaging services in New Hampshire after the state launched a website publishing health prices for most consumers with private health insurance.[32]  One study found use of a telephone- and email-based tool to search for health care prices reduced the price paid by 10 to 17 percent and reduced the prices paid for care on average by 1.6 percent.[33]  Another study of a program that provided health plan participants, beneficiaries, or enrollees with price and quality information to help select high-value imaging services found an increase in the use of lower-cost facilities.[34]  This consumer behavior prompted higher-cost facilities to lower their prices, which resulted in a 30 percent reduction in the price variation between low- and high-cost facilities.[35]  These studies, as well the numerous studies highlighted in subsequent sections of this rule, offer substantial evidence that price transparency in health care markets will result in consumer benefits similar to those that result from transparency in other markets.
